```text

Ka whawhai tonu mātou, ake, ake, ake!
the introduction of constitutional guarantees of the tino Rangatiratanga and
mana motuhake of whānau, hapū and iwi.
In addition to te implementing the Matike Mai recommendations, Te Pāti Māori
put forward the following solutions to get kickstart our reclamation of tino

1. Māori Parliament
We demand a Māori Parliament. Our right to self-governance and self-

Governance and management of programmes and funding streams for by

There is even precedence for this kind of governmental devolution – just look at
the Irish, the Scots and the Welsh. Westminster did not work for the Scots or the
Irish - Wellington definitely does not work for Māori.
2. Remove British Royal Family as Head of State
If you look at our founding covenant as a marriage between tangata whenua
and the Crown, then Te Tiriti is the child of that marriage. It’s time Tangata
Whenua to take full custody of Te Tiriti o Waitangi from the Crown.
Te Pāti Māori will remove the British Royal Family as Head of State.
This won’t mean the Crown is off the hook. If a couple gets divorced, you don’t

country by 2026.
People are hungry for change. There is a new generation who want to see
themselves reflected in our country’s identity. The status quo is no longer
```

Ka whawhai tonu mātou, ake, ake, ake!
consistent with who we are as a nation. 70,000 people signed Te Pāti Māori’s
petition which was delivered to Parliament in June 2022.
This is not about getting rid of anything or changing who we are. It’s about
reinstating the original names of this land and strengthening who we are as a
nation.
Land Back
Since 1840, the retention and return of land has been the most significant
political aspiration of Tangata Whenua, the unifying struggle of the tino

In 1975, Dame Whina Cooper’s land march ushered in an era of noho whenua

1. Foreshore and seabed
In 2011 Te Pāti Māori successfully repealed the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004,
which represented the biggest confiscation in the history of Aotearoa. While its
replacement, the Marine and Coastal Area Act (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 is an

Te Pāti Māori will repeal the Marine and Coastal Area Act and return the

2. Crown and council land

```

### Page 6

```text
Mana Motuhake Policy
Ka whawhai tonu mātou, ake, ake, ake!
The Crown has no right to retain land that was stolen from Tangata Whenua. If it
needs to use certain land blocks, it can legally purchase or lease that land from
its rightful owners.
3. Conservation land
Te Pāti Māori will return all conservation land to mana whenua.
It is immoral that the Crown refuses to return conservation and continues to
promote a racist and paternalistic view that only they can protect biodiversity.
Whānau, hapū and iwi are the kaitiaki of our own whenua, awa and moana.
Returning conservation land isn’t just the right thing to do, it makes the most
environmental sense.
4. Private land
Te Pāti Māori will introduce a first right of refusal policy for mana whenua on all
private land.
We do not think that landowners should have land forcibly purchased or taken
from them, as in many cases happened to our tupuna. However, when land is
put up for sale, it must first be offered to recognised mana whenua of that land.
While this won’t always be taken up, over time this will ensure that Tangata

the power to revolutionise Māori social, economic, and environmental
outcomes.
Te Pāti Māori will also end perpetual leases and return control of whenua to it’s

Overhauling the Te Tiriti settlement process
Te Pāti Māori will overhaul the Treaty settlement process, reforming it to create

We are clear that fundamental reform is needed to the settlement process. The
key Crown policy settings for negotiations that must change if the process is to
be durable and have the confidence of tangata whenua. We should instead look
to an ongoing process for Māori-Crown reconciliation and relationship-building.
```

```text
Mana Motuhake Policy
Ka whawhai tonu mātou, ake, ake, ake!
Te Pāti Māori will end the fiscal envelope and insert relativity clauses into all Te

We would also empower the Waitangi Tribunal by legislating to make their

historical claims to be revisited, and new claims brought, where situations have
changed or whānau, hapū or iwi groups were shut out of the original

Often groups are shut out of negotiations due the Crown’s large natural

electorates and require all local and regional councils to have both Māori wards
and mana whenua representation.
2. Parliamentary Commissioner for Te Tiriti o Waitangi

# Energy Sovereignty Policy 2026

Source: [https://img.scoop.co.nz/media/pdfs/2609/Te_Pti_Mori_Energy_Sovereignty_Policy_FINAL.pdf](https://img.scoop.co.nz/media/pdfs/2609/Te_Pti_Mori_Energy_Sovereignty_Policy_FINAL.pdf). Attached by Te Pāti Māori to its 16 Sep 2026 press release (Scoop PA2609/S00161).

Designed layouts mean page headers, side labels and table cells can appear out of visual order; consult the PDF for layout. No words were added, removed or reworded.

## Full text

### Page 1

```text
ENERGY SOVEREIGNTY POLICY 2026 | POLICY
TE PĀTI MĀORI • ENERGY SOVEREIGNTY • 1
Energy Sovereignty Policy
Executive Summary
Energy is power.
It powers our homes, our businesses, our marae, our transport and our economy. However, too
many of our people remain customers of an energy system they do not own and have little
control over.
We pay the bills. Our whenua, wai and natural resources support the system. Our communities
host the infrastructure; yet ownership, control and profit remain concentrated elsewhere.
Te Pāti Māori will change that.
Our Energy Sovereignty policy is a just transition pathway to transform who produces, owns
and benefits from energy in Aotearoa.
CUT THE POWER
Lower energy
costs for whānau
and reduce our
dependence on
fossil fuels.
BUILD THE POWER
Invest in renewable generation, storage,
infrastructure, Māori businesses, skills,
system planning and community
resilience. Connection rules and costs
must not lock smaller Māori and
community projects out of the system.
OWN THE POWER
Shift capital,
ownership and control
into the hands of
whānau, hapū, iwi and
communities.
Te Pāti Māori will establish a just transition pathway towards Energy Sovereignty by
2035.
This is not about subsidising energy consumption, it is about building assets, shifting capital
and shifting ownership. It is about moving our people from being customers of the energy
system to becoming producers, builders, investors and owners.
```

### Page 2

```text
ENERGY SOVEREIGNTY POLICY 2026 | POLICY
TE PĀTI MĀORI • ENERGY SOVEREIGNTY • 2
Context
Aotearoa is entering a major energy transformation. Homes, transport, businesses and industry
will increasingly move away from fossil fuels and towards electricity and other renewable
energy sources.
That transition will require significant investment in generation, storage, transmission,
distribution networks, infrastructure and workforce capability. It also presents one of the largest
economic opportunities of the next generation.
Greater electrification and renewable generation mean we can produce more of the energy we
need here at home, reduce our dependence on imported fossil fuels and keep more of our
energy spending circulating within Aotearoa.
But Te Pāti Māori will not support a transition that simply replaces one form of extraction with
another. We will not accept renewable infrastructure being built on or around Māori whenua
while Māori remain customers and somebody else owns the assets.
Our renewable energy future will draw on the full range of appropriate renewable resources,
including solar, wind, geothermal, hydro, bioenergy and emerging technologies, with
development subject to Te Tiriti, mana whenua authority and strong protections for the taiao.
Anchored in Te Tiriti
Energy Sovereignty is anchored in Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
There is no climate justice without Tiriti justice.
The transition to renewable energy must uphold tino rangatiratanga and must not reproduce an
economic model where value is extracted from Māori communities while ownership, decision-
making and economic benefit accumulate elsewhere.
Māori must have meaningful rights and interests in ownership, governance, investment,
development, employment, procurement, benefit sharing and decisions affecting whenua, wai
and other taonga.
The renewable transition cannot become the next extractive economy. Renewable development
must honour Te Tiriti, protect mana whenua decision-making, uphold strong environmental
standards and avoid shifting environmental harm onto mokopuna generations.
Energy transformation must strengthen both tino rangatiratanga and intergenerational Māori
wealth.
```

### Page 3

```text
ENERGY SOVEREIGNTY POLICY 2026 | POLICY
TE PĀTI MĀORI • ENERGY SOVEREIGNTY • 3
1. Cut the Power: Lower Whānau Energy Costs
Te Pāti Māori will help whānau reduce their energy costs by making it easier to produce, store
and use more of their own energy.
We will support access to:
• Solar and batteries
• Energy-efficient appliances, heating and hot water
• Home electrification and EV charging
• Long-term, low-cost and zer o-interest finance
• Rates Assistance Scheme
Renters and whānau living in social housing must also benefit from the energy transition. We
will support renter-friendly energy solutions, community batteries and stronger electrification
standards across rental and social housing.
Crown-funded housing will be expected to lead the transition, with renewable energy and
electrification increasingly built into new developments.
Te Pāti Māori will establish a government backed loan scheme to provide long-term, low-cost
finance for homeowners, Māori landowners, papakāinga, marae and community energy
projects. This will support the installation of solar, batteries, efficient heating, hot water systems,
insulation, EV charging and other upgrades that permanently cut power costs. This financing
mechanism will be delivered through an expanded Ratepayer Assistance Scheme
This is not about permanently subsidising electricity bills. It is about investing in assets that
permanently reduce them.
THE PRINCIPLE
Invest in assets that permanently reduce power bills.
This is not about permanently subsidising electricity bills. It is about building household and
community energy capability.
2. Build the Power
Te Pāti Māori will invest in the infrastructure, capability and planning required to build the
energy system Aotearoa needs.
This means building more renewable generation, strengthening transmission and distribution
networks, investing in storage, growing the Māori energy workforce and ensuring local energy
systems are planned alongside national infrastructure.
```

### Page 4

```text
ENERGY SOVEREIGNTY POLICY 2026 | POLICY
TE PĀTI MĀORI • ENERGY SOVEREIGNTY • 4
Establish a $1 Billion Energy Sovereignty Fund
ENERGY SOVEREIGNTY FUND
$1 BILLION
Capital to build Māori and community ownership of productive energy assets.
Te Pāti Māori will establish a $1 billion Energy Sovereignty Fund to build Māori and community
ownership of the energy system.
We will reinvest at the scale of the wealth currently being extracted from our homes and
communities through the electricity system, and use that capital to build productive energy
assets owned by our people.
The Fund will invest in:
• Reducing household energy costs
• Marae and papakāinga energy resilience
• Māori-owned renewable generation
• Community batteries and microgrids
• Energy infrastructure on whenua Māori
• Māori energy businesses
• Skills, apprenticeships and workforce development
• Pathways for whānau, iwi and Māori entities to own productive energy assets
Establish a National Independence Energy Plan
We will establish a National Energy Independence Plan run by a National Energy
Independence Taskforce made up of iwi, sector groups and workforce operators.
Any situation where the private market is not setting the price of power, the market is being
regulated.
A fairness framework will be mandated to regulate pricing.
Te Pāti Māori will establish a whole-of-system National Energy Plan covering generation,
storage, transmission, distribution networks, household electrification, transport, industrial
demand, resilience, workforce development and Māori and community ownership.
The Plan will identify the renewable mix Aotearoa needs, including solar, wind, geothermal,
hydro, bioenergy and emerging technologies, and ensure national infrastructure and local
energy systems are planned together.
It will identify and fund the transmission and distribution upgrades required for new renewable
generation, community energy, electrification and storage.
```

### Page 5

```text
ENERGY SOVEREIGNTY POLICY 2026 | POLICY
TE PĀTI MĀORI • ENERGY SOVEREIGNTY • 5
Build the Power
Build a Māori Energy Workforce and Industry
Te Pāti Māori will create explicit pathways for Māori businesses, workers and training providers
across construction, electrical trades, solar and battery installation, engineering, maintenance,
energy services, transport electrification and emerging technologies.
Crown-funded energy investment will actively support Māori procurement, apprenticeships and
workforce development. The transition should create businesses, careers and intergenerational
capability owned by our people.
Build Rural Energy Capability
Te Pāti Māori will support farms and rural communities to become energy producers through
on-farm generation, energy storage, rural charging and distributed energy. Rural communities
should be owners and beneficiaries of the transition, not simply consumers facing new costs.
Build the infrastructure. Build the businesses. Build the workforce. Build the
capability.
3. Own the Power: Increase Māori and Community Ownership
Participation is not sovereignty. Ownership is.
Te Pāti Māori will deliberately increase Māori and community ownership of renewable energy
infrastructure.
The Energy Sovereignty Fund will use grants, concessional finance, guarantees, equity
investment and co-investment to enable whānau, hapū, iwi, marae, Māori landowners and
communities to acquire permanent ownership stakes in productive energy assets.
Ownership pathways will include whānau ownership, hapū and iwi equity, community and co-
operative ownership, Māori-Crown co-investment, joint ventures, Māori landowner investment
and Māori-owned business investment.
Crown investment will be designed to build Māori equity, not permanent Crown ownership.
We will create stronger pathways for mana whenua to participate as owners in major renewable
developments within their rohe and ensure Crown investment supports Māori equity rather than
simply consultation.
```

### Page 6

# Whānau Pakari – Sport and Wellbeing Policy (2020 document — NOT confirmed as 2026 policy)

Source: [https://drive.google.com/file/d/1IeJ-WmT2cwdeo6noqVaSRFk55dhQGpNl/view](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1IeJ-WmT2cwdeo6noqVaSRFk55dhQGpNl/view). Google Drive file 'MP Sport Policy.pdf' linked from maoriparty.org.nz/maori_sports (page captured March 2026). PDF metadata: created 30 Aug 2020 — an earlier election's policy, included for reference only.

> Extraction notes: text is reproduced in the PDF's content-stream order, page by page. Only whitespace and glyph markup were normalised (bullet glyphs shown as •, decorative icons removed). Designed layouts mean page headers, side labels and table cells can appear out of visual order; consult the PDF for layout. No words were added, removed or reworded.

## Full text

### Page 1

```text
Whānau Pakari – Sport and Wellbeing Policy
Executive Summary
He Whānau Pakari e ora ai te tangata – Mai rā anō i te whitinga mai ki Aotearoa kua pakari te tīnana,
te hinengaro me te wairua. Me hoki anō tātau kia tū hei whānau pakari, hei whānau ora.
The Māori Party acknowledges that exercise has been a big part of who we are, how we came
here and how we would traverse the lands of Aotearoa. Māori invented many sports prior to
European arrival. Running, Swimming, Fishing, Waka, Hunting, Kī o Rahi, Taiaha/Mau rakau/Te
Whare Tū Taua, to name a few - all examples of a tūpuna mindset, an ancestral way of being and
acting which we call – Whānau Pakari. The ability to exercise and strive for excellence. Whānau
Pakari is part of our Oranga Tangata policy framework.
There is much to be taught and learnt from the navigators of our past and how we can use that
mātauranga to sail and paddle our way into a future frame by Whānau Pakari. It is a known fact
that Māori genetic makeup is stronger than others. When there is commitment, dedication, and
great support around Māori to achieve a high standard in sport, it is guaranteed that Māori will
thrive.
Our ancestors were not just athletic they were also strategic thinkers with intentions to survive.
This all required, stamina, resilience, endurance, speed, agility, and logic. There is great
opportunity to showcase the sporting talent of Māori on the world stage. Nurturing pathways for
our mokopuna and tamariki to aspire to and offer pathways into education opportunities.
The Māori Party will;
1. Establish and fund a National Māori Sporting body, targeting Māori sporting codes and
sports with high Māori participation
2. Establish a $100M Whānau Pakari fund for 3-years to invest into Māori sporting codes
a. Funding Māori sporting academies that incorporate Whānau Pakari principles
b. Funding scholarships to ensure that barriers for Māori are eliminated and to
allow their potential to shine
c. Funding iwi & hapū Pā Wars events
d. Upskilling volunteers and coaches in sporting codes with high Māori participation
3. Ensure that funds go directly to the regional Māori sporting codes for Māori, by Māori
and not via regional sporting bodies
```

### Page 2

```text
4. Ensure sporting codes with high Māori participation have Māori governing boards,
allowing them to individually compete at world cup events as Aotearoa Māori
5. Provide a Māori Sports mentoring programme; delivering tertiary education
opportunities & career pathways for life beyond the sporting field
Context
In the early 19th
century, Europeans bought new sports to NZ. Some became more popular with
Māori than others. In 1883 Māori boxer Herbert Slade fought the American heavyweight
champion in New York and lost but became a celebrity. Too often Māori have to travel to other
countries to live to be recognised on the world stage. We want them to stay in their homeland
and represent their country as tangata whenua of this country under the banner of Aotearoa
Māori. In the early 20th
century, Māori formed their own teams. Māori sporting associations were
founded in various sports. The first official national Māori rugby team was selected in 1910 prior
to George Nepia playing for the All Blacks. Rugby League and Hockey were other popular sports
codes for Māori. From the 20th
century, Golf, Cricket, Tennis, Hockey, netball, Touch rugby, Waka
Ama, Football, Squash, Basketball & Golden Shears saw many Māori represent on the world
stage. It is only through a coordinated Māori centred approach that we can revive collective and
individual Māori success through Whānau Pakari.
Māori sporting codes have survived on pure grit and determination to keep these codes alive.
You will often find a couple of parents who are key drivers that will more than likely be pulling
money out of their own wallets to ensure theirs and other tamariki in their regions get to
represent their codes and eliminate the financial burden. A specific Māori fund through Whānau
Pakari will ensure those burdens are reduced heavily or eliminated. We cannot afford to lose our
place in the sporting world. It has been quoted by some Māori that have represented on the
world stage that if there was a Māori world stage team in their particular code that they would’ve
wanted to represent in that team.
Our Māori boarding school pupils were high contributors to many of the sporting representation
on the world stage. As the existence of such schools has declined so too has our representation.
Nowadays, we have parents applying more than just sports to the game. These parents hold the
young tamariki accountable, set goals, offer employment to get them giving back to the sport
(coach, referee), up skill them and travel opportunities because they see the potential our Māori
tamariki have. This is not exclusive to any particular Māori sporting code, you will find this in
every Māori sporting code.
Too many of our tamariki miss the opportunities in sport because of the financial burden placed
on their families will give up and turn to drugs and gangs. Sport is the alternative for many
keeping them busy and offering them opportunities to travel and be better, see the world and
give them the confidence our tamariki rightfully deserve in their own country.
```

### Mana Hauā - Disability

Mana Hauā relates to the life force and the inherent value of Māori disabled.

Whānau Hauā and Māori disabled are terms used in relation to whānau with physical, mental, intellectual, or sensory impairments.

Te Pāti Māori dreams and aspirations are to achieve tino rangatiratanga for whānau, hapū and iwi. This policy is a strength based kaupapa that recognises Mana Hauā and seeks to assert the rights and wellbeing of Whānau Hauā within our whānau, hapū and iwi.

Te Pāti Māori will:

- Establish a Mana Hauā Authority

- Reallocate 25% of all Disability funding to the Māna Hauā Authority

- Establish Kaupapa Māori disability organisations and rehabilitation facilities.

- Abolish ACC and establish a Māori ACC Authority.

- Ensure that Māori disability organisations are formally included in the development of all disability-related policy and legislation.

- Reform building standards to require that all new housing builds are fully accessible.

- Remove all barriers for Tangata Hauā to access health services

- Ensure that antenatal screening programmes are not biased towards termination of pregnancies if a disability is diagnosed.

- Recognise Te Reo Rotarota as an official language in Aotearoa.

- Require te reo Māori proficiency to be assessed in NZSL qualifications.

- Provide pathways for te reo Māori speakers to learn Te Reo Rotarota and NZSL.

- Abolish abatement rates on benefits for Tangata Hauā and their careworkers.

- Immediately abolish the minimum wage exemption for Tangata Hauā.

This is not about Parliament giving Te Tiriti its authority. Parliament did not create Te Tiriti; it is about binding the Crown to the promises it already made and ensuring that no future government can simply choose to walk away from them. To read the full policy Click here

### Tax

Tax - Click to read more

What we’ll do Make sure the wealthiest pay their fair share. Use that revenue to fund housing, health, education and whānau support. Why it matters When the system rewards the top and squeezes everyone else, poverty becomes permanent. A country that protects the wealthy while whānau go without is not fair, it is rigged. Tax is one of the ways we return power, resources, and opportunity back to the people who keep this country moving. To read the full policy Click here

### Mana Takatāpui

Mana Takatāpui - Click to read more

What we’ll do Protect the wellbeing, safety, and dignity of takatāpui Māori. Make sure public services are inclusive, accessible, and accountable. Why it matters Takatāpui Māori deserve to live safely and fully as themselves; without discrimination, exclusion, or harm. Takatāpui Māori deserve to live with safety, dignity, joy, and full belonging in their whānau, hapori, and nation. No one should be pushed to the margins for being wholly themselves. To read the full policy. Click here

### Kai Sovereignty

Kai Sovereignty - Click to read more

What we’ll do Protect Māori food systems (including seed sovereignty, rejecting GE foods, and upholding WAI262). Invest in community food systems and regenerative Māori agriculture. Break corporate control by supporting Māori-owned supermarkets and protecting local kai sellers. Increase access to land for food production. Why it matters Aotearoa grows enough kai to feed everyone, yet too many whānau are goinghungry. That is not scarcity, it is system failure. Kai sovereignty means affordable,healthy kai connected to whenua, whakapapa, and Māori control. To read the full policy Click here

### Mokopuna Māori

Mokopuna Māori - Click to read more

What we’ll do End the pipeline that removes Māori children from their people. Restore whānau authority and invest in whānau-led care. Make the state accountable for harm caused through uplifts and placements. Why it matters Our tamariki are not state problems to be managed. They are whakapapa, promise, and future leaders born to thrive. Protecting mokopuna Māori means restoring whānau authority and ending the systems that separate our children from their people. To read the full policy. Click here

### Disabilities

Disabilities - Click to read more

What we’ll do Support Māori-led disability services and decision-making. Make support easier to access and less degrading. Fund support that fits whānau realities, not bureaucratic categories. Why it matters Disabled Māori deserve support that honours their mana, their whānau, and their right to live fully. No one should have to fight a degrading system just to access the care, dignity, and support they are entitled to. To read the full policy. Click here

### Housing

Housing - Click to read more

What we’ll do Build and support more public and affordable homes. Make it easier to build homes on Māori/ancestral land. Stop speculation and land-banking (including action on vacant properties). Why it matters A warm, safe, secure home is not a luxury. It is the ground everything else stands on: health, education, safety, stability, and hope. Our people deserve homes, not waiting lists, overcrowding, or speculation. To read the full policy. Click here

### Education & Training

Education & Training - Click to read more

What we’ll do Build Māori-led education authority and solutions. Embed mātauranga Māori properly across learning. Remove barriers that block whānau from education and training. Support Māori governance and decision-making in education. Why it matters Education should never teach our tamariki to leave themselves at the door. It should strengthen identity, grow confidence, open pathways, and prepare our people to lead in the world as Māori.

### Toi Māori

Toi Māori - Click to read more

What we’ll do Invest in Toi Māori and Māori creative industries. Protect Māori cultural rights and expressions. Back Māori-led arts infrastructure, funding, and pathways. Why it matters Toi Māori is not decoration. It is truth-telling, resistance, healing, identity, and legacy. Our art carries the stories others tried to silence and projects our imagination into the future. To read the full policy. Click here

### Te Reo Māori

Te Reo Māori - Click to read more

What we’ll do Strengthen te reo Māori and normalise it everywhere. Invest in te reo Māori learning pathways and community-led language revitalisation. Make sure the state is accountable for protecting te reo Māori. Why it matters Te reo Māori is not just a language. It is identity, memory, authority, and the sound of our survival. When te reo thrives, our people stand taller and our nation becomes more honest about who it is. To read the full policy. Click here

### Health

Health - Click to read more

What we’ll do Re-build and strengthen Māori-led health authority and solutions. Shift the system toward prevention and whānau wellbeing, not just crisis response. Make services accessible, culturally safe, and accountable to Māori. Why it matters A health system that does not understand Māori will keep failing Māori. Our people deserve care that sees the whole person, strengthens whānau, prevents harm, and is accountable to the communities it serves. To read the full policy. Click here

### Mana Motuhake

Mana Motuhake - Click to read more

What we’ll do Commit to Te Tiriti-based constitutional change. Strengthen Māori political authority and governance structures. Progress land back and rangatiratanga commitments under Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Why it matters Without constitutional transformation, every gain our people make can be undone by the next government. Mana motuhake means power must return to where it belongs: with tangata whenua, hapū, iwi, whānau, and our people. To read the full policy. Click here

### Sports

Sports - Click to read more

What we’ll do Invest in sport and community initiatives that build belonging, wellbeing, and opportunity. Support pathways for rangatahi through local clubs, programmes, and facilities. Why it matters Sport is more than a game. It builds belonging, discipline, leadership, confidence, and connection. Strong clubs and community pathways give our rangatahi places to stand, people to stand with, and futures to run toward. To read the full policy. Click here

### Justice

Justice - Click to read more

What we’ll do Build Māori-led justice authority and community solutions. Reform laws that criminalise poverty and survival. Move away from mass imprisonment and toward long-term transformation. Why it matters A system that cages Māori generation after generation is not failing by accident. True justice means ending the machinery that criminalises poverty, trauma, and survival, and building Māori-led solutions that restore mana, safety, and futures. To read the full policy. Click here

### Economic development

Economic development - Click to read more

What we’ll do Build Māori-led institutions and funds that grow Māori enterprise. Support trade, innovation, and long-term Māori wealth building. Protect Māori data and knowledge (data sovereignty). Why it matters Māori prosperity cannot rely on permission from systems built to exclude us. Economic power is political power. This is about restoring what was taken, growing Māori wealth, and building a future where our people thrive on our own terms. To read the full policy. Click here

### Cost of living

Cost of living - Click to read more

What we’ll do Lift incomes so people can live with dignity. Strengthen welfare so whānau aren’t punished for being poor. Back practical cost-of-living relief (including transport affordability). Why it matters When whānau can’t meet the basics, everything else around them breaks - their health, their learning, their stability and their safety. No whānau should be forced to choose between kai, rent, power, transport, medicine, or school costs. When the basics become unaffordable, dignity is stripped away. We will fight for an economy where our people can live, not just survive. To read the full policy. Click here

### Military neutrality

Military neutrality - Click to read more

What we’ll do Declare Aotearoa a militarily neutral nation. Reset foreign policy to be independent, grounded in Māori values, and centred on Pacific and Indigenous relationships. Review and withdraw from military alignments that undermine sovereignty. Refocus the Defence Force on protection, disaster response, and Pacific support. Uphold international human rights and hold war criminals to account. Why it matters Neutrality is mana motuhake in action. Our sovereignty shouldn’t be dictated by foreign Neutrality is mana motuhake in action. Our foreign policy should not be dictated by powerful nations, military alliances, or wars that are not ours. Aotearoa must stand for peace, justice, Indigenous solidarity, and Pacific protection. To read the full policy. Click here

### Freshwater Policy

Freshwater Policy - Click to read more

What we’ll do Assert Māori rights and authority over freshwater. Stop decisions being made without Māori consent. Ensure resources are protected and benefits are shared fairly. Why it matters Water is life. It carries whakapapa, sustains our whenua, feeds our people, and binds generations together. Decisions about wai must sit with those who have carried responsibility for it since time immemorial. To read the full policy. Click here

### Climate

Climate - Click to read more

What we’ll do Protect whenua and moana from extractive industries (including banning seabed mining). Invest in climate resilience for communities most at risk. Back regenerative and sustainable approaches aligned with Māori values. Why it matters Our whenua, awa, moana, marae, wāhi tapu, mahinga kai and whakapapa are not resources to be exploited. They are our inheritance, our responsibility, and our future. Climate justice is about protecting our right to live safely, affordably, and sovereign on our own whenua. To read the full policy. ## Full text

### We Want Cheaper Power And We Want Our People To Own It.

Published by Te Pāti Māori

September 16, 2026

Te Pāti Māori has today announced its Energy Sovereignty policy, a plan to cut power costs, build Aotearoa’s energy future and shift ownership into the hands of whānau, hapū, iwi and communities.

“Every party is talking about generating more electricity. We’re asking the question they keep avoiding: who will own it?” said Te Pāti Co-Leader Rawiri Waititi

“If we replace fossil fuels with renewables but leave ownership and profits concentrated in the same hands, we haven’t transformed the system. We’ve just changed the technology.

“Participation is not sovereignty. Ownership is.”

Te Pāti Māori will:

- Establish a $1 billion Energy Sovereignty Fund to build Māori and community-owned energy assets.

- Develop a long-term National Energy Plan.

- Give regulators stronger powers to act against excessive pricing and profits.

- Establish fair value so whānau and communities are properly paid for the energy they generate and store.

- Set a pathway to Energy Sovereignty by 2035.

Co-Leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer said the renewable transition cannot become the next extractive economy.

“Our whenua, wai and resources have generated wealth for others for generations. We will not allow that history to repeat itself under a green label.

“We want whānau generating power, marae storing it, iwi owning generation, Māori businesses building it and the wealth staying in our communities.

“Other parties want to build more power. We want our people to own it.

Cut the Power. Build the Power. Own the Power. Power to the people.”

# “What matters to you?” policy tool (content from the Te Pāti Māori Policy Manifesto 2026)

Source: <https://www.maoriparty.org.nz/what-matters-to-you> — Common Crawl capture 2026-10-08T18:53:45Z

## Full text

## Part 1 — policies by area (“Pick your top three”)


### Money in my pocket (Pūtea)

*No one should be paid less than what it costs to live.*

- **No tax on the first $30,000 you earn** — Less tax for 97% of people. Nine in ten people get around $4,000 more a year on average.
- **The minimum wage goes straight up to the living wage** — That's $28.95 an hour. Youth rates and starting out rates end.
- **GST off kai, paid back to you as a tax credit** — For anyone earning $60,000 or less. Worth up to eight weeks of kai every year. Around 3 million people get it.
- **Double baseline benefits** — Remove sanctions and work test obligations, and cancel benefit debt owed to the Crown.
- **Free public transport** — Free right away for tamariki, students and Community Services Card holders. Half price for everyone else, then free for everyone within five years.
- **Lower power bills** — Help for whānau with solar, batteries, better heating, and low cost or zero interest finance.
- **Break the supermarket duopoly** — $100 million to help Māori collectives set up their own supermarket chains.
- **Company tax back to 33%** — And a 5% tax on profits sent offshore.
- **Get paid fairly for power you make** — If you generate or store power and send it back to the grid, you get a fair price for it.
- **Protect workers** — Pay equity for Māori, and stronger union rights and collective bargaining.

### A warm and safe home (Kāinga)

*Everyone has the right to a warm, dry and secure home.*

- **Freeze rents** — After the freeze, rents can only go up by inflation each year, unless the owner makes big improvements.
- **End no cause evictions in our first 100 days** — More security for whānau who rent.
- **Build 2,000 homes on ancestral Māori land within four years** — Built by Māori workers, apprentices and trainees, supporting papakāinga.
- **Build more state houses and stop selling them off cheap to investors**
- **Half of all new social housing goes to whānau Māori** — Māori make up half the social housing waiting list.
- **End youth homelessness** — A new agency, Rangatahi Ora, and a legal duty on government to help any young person without a home.
- **Tax homes left empty** — A 2% yearly tax on homes left empty for more than three months.
- **Every new government build made accessible for all whānau**

### Our tamariki and mokopuna (Mokopuna)

*Mokopuna Māori raised with love, safety, identity and belonging.*

- **End state care of mokopuna Māori** — Replace it with care led by Māori and grounded in whakapapa. End uplifting pēpi and mokopuna without whānau, hapū and iwi consent.
- **A Mokopuna Māori Authority** — Takes over the care and protection of mokopuna Māori from Oranga Tamariki, with about $1 billion a year moved across to it.
- **Free school lunches in every kura and public school**
- **Free counselling in schools** — And mental wellbeing becomes a core part of what's taught.
- **Carry out all 138 recommendations from the Royal Commission into Abuse in Care**
- **Close military style bootcamps straight away** — Youth justice residences closed by 2030.
- **Free public transport for tamariki**
- **Every law and policy decision must uphold the rights of mokopuna** — Their right to their language and culture, good health, education, and a voice in decisions about them.

### Learning and training (Ako)

*Māori learners thrive when Māori lead.*

- **A Māori Education Authority** — Long term, stable funding for kōhanga reo, kura kaupapa Māori, wharekura and wānanga.
- **A Te Kōhanga Reo Act, with guaranteed funding every year** — Plus $20 million a year for buildings and a one off $50 million for the roughly 80 kōhanga reo needing new builds or upgrades.
- **$1.25 billion over five years for kura property** — That is $250 million every year to develop kura and grow Māori medium education.
- **Te reo Māori a core subject from primary school to Year 10** — Plus compulsory teaching of Aotearoa history, tikanga and te ao Māori.
- **Te Ahu o Te Reo Māori restored** — Funded at $30 million a year.
- **20 new kōhanga reo over three years** — Built with the Trust setting the priorities.
- **Write off the living cost part of every student loan** — And work towards full write offs for people who live and work here for five years.
- **A student allowance for every student, at double the rate** — Scrap the parental income test, and restore allowances for postgraduate, part time and long course students.
- **Free public transport for all students, including tertiary**
- **Teachers' pay rises that keep up with inflation** — Support for Māori teachers, kaiako and support staff, and action on pay and workload.
- **Second chance and adult education**
- **Scholarships and trade pathways** — Kai sovereignty scholarships for rangatahi in food science, marine biology and primary industries, and apprenticeships in building and energy.

### Being well (Oranga)

*Māori die seven years earlier than non Māori. That has to change.*

- **Free doctor visits and free dental care for all whānau** — Free primary healthcare and free dental care.
- **$500 million a year for kaupapa Māori mental health** — Plus free mental health services in the community, and addiction treated as a health issue.
- **Clinics on marae and mobile health units** — And free delivery of medication.
- **Earlier bowel screening** — From age 45 for everyone, and from 35 for Māori and Pacific peoples.
- **Māori leading Māori health** — A quarter of all health and ACC funding moved to systems led by Māori.
- **A Mana Hauā Authority led by Māori for disabled whānau** — Support that keeps Tangata Hauā with their whānau, and recognises unpaid care as real work.
- **Protect rongoā Māori and fund more medicines through PHARMAC**
- **Gender affirming healthcare in the public system** — Led by takatāpui and culturally safe, with protection for intersex tamariki from gender normalising surgery.

### Our whenua, wai and moana (Taiao)

*When the land is harmed, the people are harmed.*

- **Ban seabed mining** — End new oil and gas exploration, and support workers through a fair change.
- **Repeal the Fast Track Approvals Act** — And cancel mining consents that were fast tracked.
- **End mining on conservation land**
- **Safe, affordable drinking water for every whānau** — And no selling or trading of water rights. Water is a taonga, not a product.
- **Mana whenua decide about freshwater** — End Crown only control of water.
- **$1 billion to put solar and insulation on marae, kura, papakāinga and homes**
- **Marae and hapū funded as hubs for disasters** — Plus a $100 million fund to rebuild and clean up marae, urupā and papakāinga.
- **$400 million to help Māori farmers move to regenerative farming** — Including small, diverse whenua blocks growing kai for local people.
- **A $100 million Community Kai Fund** — For home gardens, marae māra kai, and food farms led by Māori and communities.

### Our reo and who we are (Tuakiri)

*Te reo Māori should be part of everyday life, not something you have to ask for.*

- **Te reo Māori compulsory in education** — And public agencies required to work in both languages.
- **Fund reo led by whānau and marae** — Support iwi language plans and protect our regional dialects.
- **Stronger Māori media and broadcasting in te reo**
- **$19 million base funding for Te Matatini** — Plus $10 million for kapa haka in communities, hapū and iwi.
- **A Toi Māori authority led by Māori** — Funded the same as Creative NZ, plus a guaranteed income scheme for artists.
- **A $100 million Whānau Pakari fund for sport** — Māori sports academies, scholarships for Māori athletes, and funding for Pā Wars.
- **Māori teams competing overseas as Aotearoa Māori**
- **Pathways for takatāpui into te reo fluency and leadership on marae** — And funding for creative and cultural expression led by takatāpui.

### Making our own decisions (Mana motuhake)

*Te Tiriti can't be settled. It's a living agreement that must be honoured.*

- **Land back** — Return the foreshore and seabed, conservation land, and Crown and council land to mana whenua.
- **Make Waitangi Tribunal recommendations binding on the Crown**
- **An independent Te Tiriti Commission** — With the power to stop Crown decisions that seriously breach Te Tiriti.
- **Protect the Māori seats for good** — Entrench the Māori electorates and require Māori wards in every council.
- **A quarter of all government spending on contracts goes to Māori businesses** — Plus a $4.5 billion fund to grow Māori land, marae and business.
- **Overseas buyers can lease our land but never own it**
- **Māori data controlled by Māori**

### Justice and safety (Tika)

*Justice is about balance and healing, not just punishment.*

- **An independent Māori Justice Authority** — Funded with half of the Corrections, Police and Courts budgets.
- **Abolish prisons by 2040** — Replaced with community based, restorative alternatives grounded in tikanga. Keeping people safe through prevention, not punishment.
- **Drug use treated as a health issue, not a crime** — Convictions for drug use and possession wiped, and double the funding to prevent and treat alcohol and drug harm.
- **Legal help led by Māori** — Independent Māori legal aid, kaupapa Māori community law centres, and more support for Māori Wardens.
- **Raise the age of criminal responsibility from 10 to 16**
- **Body cameras for every police officer** — And a truly independent police watchdog grounded in te ao Māori.
- **Repeal three strikes and the gang laws**
- **Lower the voting age to 16** — Enrol any time, and switch between the Māori and general rolls any time.
- **Aotearoa becomes a neutral country** — No fighting in foreign wars unless we're directly threatened. The Defence Force focuses on disaster response and the Pacific.

## Part 2 — what changes for you (“Which of these sounds like you or your whānau?”)


### Renting

- **Rents frozen** — Then only allowed to rise by inflation each year.
- **No more no cause evictions** — Gone in our first 100 days.

### Working for wages

- **No tax on your first $30,000**
- **Minimum wage raised to the living wage** — $28.95 an hour.

### Money's tight

- **GST off kai, paid back to you as a tax credit** — If you earn $60,000 or less. Worth up to eight weeks of kai a year.
- **A $100 million Community Kai Fund** — For home gardens and marae māra kai.

### On a benefit

- **Baseline benefits doubled** — Sanctions and work test obligations removed.
- **Benefit debt to the Crown cancelled** — And hardship grants that don't need to be paid back.
- **Special Needs Grants that cover cultural costs** — Including tangihanga and unveilings.

### Studying

- **Living cost part of your student loan written off**
- **A student allowance for every student, at double the rate** — And free public transport for students, including tertiary.

### Tamariki or mokopuna at home

- **Free lunches at every kura and public school**
- **Free counselling in schools**
- **Free public transport for tamariki**

### Rangatahi

- **Youth pay rates scrapped** — You get the living wage like everyone else.
- **A legal duty to end youth homelessness**
- **Voting age lowered to 16**

### Working in education

- **Pay rises that keep up with inflation** — For all teachers.
- **Support for Māori teachers, kaiako and support staff** — And action on pay inequity and workload.

### Health or mental health challenges

- **Free doctor visits and free dental care for all whānau**
- **$500 million a year for kaupapa Māori mental health** — Plus free mental health services in the community.
- **Addiction treated as a health issue** — With double the funding for prevention, harm reduction and treatment for alcohol and drug harm.

### Kaumātua

- **Free doctor visits and free dental care**
- **Free delivery of medication, and clinics on marae**

### Disability and carers

- **A Mana Hauā Authority led by Māori**
- **Unpaid care recognised as real work** — And disability support aligned with income so no one is forced into poverty.

### Takatāpui

- **$200 million over three years for takatāpui** — Including gender affirming healthcare in the public system, safe housing, and education safety programmes.
- **An independent Takatāpui Commission** — Governed by takatāpui, with guaranteed yearly funding no minister can hold back.
- **The Human Rights Act updated** — To protect people of diverse genders, sexualities and sex characteristics.
